canonical_topic: Electricity storage as a price-arbitrage opportunity
definition: The idea that if electricity could be stored cheaply and efficiently, it could be bought during low-price periods and resold during high-price periods, exploiting the market's recurring day/night price swings.
core_idea: Electricity prices repeat a daily pattern of cheap overnight power and expensive daytime power; storage that could capture this spread would be highly profitable, which is why efficient storage is described as a major prize for electrical markets — but in practice available technology is not efficient enough to make this simple arbitrage broadly economical.
key_points: Electricity prices oscillate predictably, typically highest during the day and lowest at night and on weekends.
If storage were cheap and efficient, buying overnight and reselling the next day would be a straightforward profit strategy.
Storage would change electrical market behavior substantially if it were efficient enough to support this kind of resale.
In practice, storage technology is generally not efficient enough for this type of trading to work economically.
relationships: Round-trip efficiency sets storage breakeven economics
trading_implications: Storage value should be modeled around the size and reliability of the peak-vs-off-peak price spread available in the market.
A storage arbitrage strategy is a bet that the spread persists and is large enough to cover round-trip losses plus capital and operating costs.
caveats: Cheap storage sounds like an easy arbitrage, but low round-trip efficiency plus installation/maintenance costs can eliminate the apparent profit.
